Abbreviations: CI: Confidence Interval F-75: Therapeutic milk used during the stabilization phase of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) treatment F-100: Therapeutic milk used during the transition and recovery phases of SAM treatment IQR: Interquartile Range MUAC: Mid-Upper Arm Circumference NCHS: National Center for Health Statistics NGO: Non-Governmental Organization OTP: Outpatient Treatment Program PICO: Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcomes RCT: Randomized Controlled Trial RUTF: Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food SAM: Severe Acute Malnutrition SD: Standard Deviation SFP: Supplementary Feeding Programme W/H: Weight-for-Height WHM: Weight-for-Height Percentage of the Median WHO: World Health Organization WHO-GS: World Health Organization Child Growth Standards WHZ: Weight-for-Height Z-Score Measurements: cm: Centimeter day: Day g: Gram kcal: Kilocalorie kg: Kilogram kJ: Kilojoule m: Month ml: Milliliter mm: Millimeter n: Number w: Week Abstract: Background: A low mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) of less than 115 mm is increasingly being used as a standalone anthropometric criterion for admitting severely acutely malnourished (SAM) children into nutritional rehabilitation programs. This is often used alongside a low weight-for-height z-score (WHZ) of less than -3. However, these two indicators correlate poorly. This study reviewed evidence on the comparative outcomes of children with SAM admitted and discharged from nutritional rehabilitation programs based on either MUAC or WHZ. The use of bilateral pitting edema as an independent indicator of SAM was not included in the scope of this review. Methods: A systematic search was conducted in Medline, Embase, CRD databases, the Cochrane Library, and grey literature. The search focused on evidence related to mortality, recovery, treatment duration, costs, adverse events, and population coverage when SAM admission was based on MUAC versus WHZ. Findings: Eleven studies were included in the review. Only one cohort study directly compared children with a MUAC <115 mm and those with a WHZ <-3 at the start of nutritional rehabilitation. This study reported similar mortality rates in both groups, although the underlying causes of mortality may differ. Children with low MUAC were more likely to be younger, female, stunted, and present with nutritional edema compared to those with low WHZ. Four studies admitted SAM children based solely on MUAC criteria. One study reported slower daily MUAC gains in younger, smaller children and females. Two studies discharged children based on MUAC thresholds (e.g., MUAC ≥124 mm or MUAC ≥130 mm) but did not report post-discharge outcomes. The optimal MUAC cut-off for discharge remains unknown. No studies reported on costs, adverse effects, or population coverage. Additionally, no studies assessed the outcomes of children with low WHZ who were excluded from treatment due to not meeting the MUAC-only admission criteria. Conclusion: There is evidence suggesting that MUAC could be used as a standalone criterion for admitting and discharging SAM children from nutritional rehabilitation programs. However, the current evidence base is insufficient. More data are needed, particularly on the risks faced by children with low WHZ who are not treated for SAM when MUAC is used as the sole criterion. The influence of factors such as age, sex, and stunting on rehabilitation outcomes in children admitted with MUAC <115 mm also requires further clarification. Numerous active nutritional programs worldwide could provide valuable data through thorough evaluation in the short term. This work was commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO). Background and Objective: In 1999, the World Health Organization (WHO) defined severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in children aged 6–59 months as a weight-for-height z-score (WHZ) of less than -3 standard deviations (SD) (severe wasting) or the presence of bilateral pitting edema. The reference population used at the time was the 1978 NCHS reference until the release of the 2006 WHO Child Growth Standards (WHO-GS). In 2007, United Nations agencies endorsed a low mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) of less than 110 mm as an independent diagnostic criterion for SAM, alongside WHZ <-3 or nutritional edema. This MUAC cut-off was later increased to <115 mm to better align with the WHZ <-3 classification under the 2006 WHO-GS. MUAC has operational advantages over WHZ. It does not require reference charts, as a single cut-off is applied regardless of sex, age, or height. It requires only one measurement using a simple and inexpensive arm strip. The color-coded bands on the strip can be easily interpreted by community workers with limited education, making it suitable for large community-based programs. Since its endorsement by the United Nations and due to its operational advantages, MUAC is increasingly being used as a standalone admission criterion for nutritional rehabilitation in countries such as Bangladesh, Ethiopia, and Pakistan. However, MUAC-based and WHZ-based malnutrition diagnoses correlate poorly. Only about 40% of children identified as SAM by one indicator are also diagnosed as such by the other. This discrepancy poses significant programmatic challenges and confusion. Relying on only one indicator may under-detect true acute malnutrition cases, while using both indicators could inflate program volumes unnecessarily. A related question concerns the choice of anthropometric indicators for monitoring nutritional rehabilitation and deciding discharge. Historically, SAM in children aged 6–59 months was considered a condition requiring systematic inpatient treatment. The recommended anthropometric discharge criterion was based on WHZ ≥-1 or weight-for-height (W/H) ≥90% of the reference median. It has also been proposed that children be discharged based on percent weight gain (>15% of the weight at enrollment). However, when admission is based on MUAC alone, it may be practical to use MUAC for monitoring recovery, particularly in community-based programs. Historical cohort studies from Bangladesh, Malawi, and Uganda suggest that the mortality risk does not exceed 1/10,000/day if MUAC ≥125 mm. Consequently, this cut-off has been proposed to define nutritional recovery. However, outcomes of children discharged based on MUAC alone must be reviewed before issuing guidance. To address these issues, this study reviewed evidence on the outcomes of SAM children admitted to and discharged from nutritional rehabilitation programs based on MUAC as a standalone criterion compared to WHZ. The use of bilateral pitting edema as an independent indicator of SAM was outside the scope of this review.
